q-126742.name: Question 1
q-126742.problem: Find a vector that's tangent to the curve $r(t)=⟨3-2{t}^{2},-{e}^{-t}⟩$ at the point where $t=0.$
q-126742.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=0,$ the vector ${r}^{′}(0)$ is tangent to the curve.

Let's calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3-2{t}^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{e}^{-t})⟩ \\  & =⟨-4t,{e}^{-t}⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =⟨-4(0),{e}^{-0}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point where $t=0$ is $⟨0,1⟩.$

At the point where t=0, the vector r′(0) is tangent to the curve.

q-126741.name: Question 2
q-126741.problem: Find a vector that's tangent to the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{3}-1,{t}^{2}+1⟩$ at the point where $t=-2.$
q-126741.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=-2,$ the vector ${r}^{′}(-2)$ is tangent to the curve.

Let's calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=-2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2},2t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(-2) & =⟨3(-2)^{2},2(-2)⟩ \\  & =⟨12,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point where $t=-2$ is $⟨12,-4⟩.$

q-75198.name: Question 3
q-75198.problem: Find a tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=\operatorname{sec}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,j+t\,k$ at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$
q-75198.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$,  the vector ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})$ is tangent to the curve.

Let's calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sec}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{tan}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,k \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,i+{sec}^{2}⁡t\,j+\,k \\ {r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\operatorname{sec}⁡\frac{\pi }{4}\operatorname{tan}⁡\frac{\pi }{4}\,i+{sec}^{2}⁡\frac{\pi }{4}\,j+\,k \\  & =\sqrt{2}\,i+2\,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$  is  $\sqrt{2}\,i+2\,j+\,k.$

q-126834.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=⟨1-4{t}^{2},5t+1⟩$ at the point where $t=-1,$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
q-126834.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=-1,$ the vector ${r}^{′}(-1)$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as
 

$$
R(u)=r(-1)+u{r}^{′}(-1),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨1-4(-1)^{2},5(-1)+1⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-4{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5t+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-8t,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=-1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(-1) & =⟨-8(-1),5⟩ \\  & =⟨8,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where $t=-1$ is

$$
R(u)=⟨-3,-4⟩+u⟨8,5⟩,\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

q-32920.name: Question 7
q-32920.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve  $r(t)=\sqrt{1+t}\,i+({t}^{2}-5)\,j+(3t-1)\,k$ at the point $P(2,4,8),$  valid for all real values of $u?$
q-32920.worked_solution:
The point $P(2,4,8)$ is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

$$
R(u)=r({t}_{0})+u\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

where ${t}_{0}$ corresponds to the value of $t$ at the point $P.$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =2\,i+4\,j+8\,k \\ \sqrt{1+t}\,i+({t}^{2}-5)\,j+(3t-1)\,k & =2\,i+4\,j+8\,k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1+t}=2 \\ {t}^{2}-5=4 \\ 3t-1=8\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the third equation, we get $t=3.$ This value also satifies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(2,4,8)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(3).$  

We calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{1+t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-5)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t-1)\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1+t}}\,i+2t\,j+3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(3) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1+(3)}}\,i+2(3)\,j+3\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{4}}\,i+2\cdot 3\,j+3\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\,i+6\,j+3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point $P(2,4,8)$ is

$$
R(u)=2i+4\,j+8\,k+u(\frac{1}{4}\,i+6\,j+3\,k),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

q-32920.html:
Question 7
?

Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve r(t)=1+ti+(t2−5)j+(3t−1)k at the point P(2,4,8), valid for all real values of u?

a
2i+4j+8k+u(14i−6j−3k)
b
2i+4j+8k+u(i+6j+6k)
c
2i+4j+8k+u(14i+6j+3k)
d
2i+4j+8k+u(i+6j+3k)
e
2i+4j+8k+u(14i+3j−3k)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The point P(2,4,8) is at the tip of r(t) for some specific value t0 of the parameter t. At this point the vector r′(t0) is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at P can be parametrized as

R(u)=r(t0)+ur′(t0),u∈(−∞,∞),

where t0 corresponds to the value of t at the point P.

First, we find the value of t that corresponds to P. We know that:

r(t)=2i+4j+8k1+ti+(t2−5)j+(3t−1)k=2i+4j+8k,

and equating the coefficients of i,j, and k yields the following system:

{1+t=2t2−5=43t−1=8

From the third equation, we get t=3. This value also satifies the other two equations. Therefore, P(2,4,8) is at the tip of the vector r(3).

We calculate r′(t):
r′(t)=ddt(1+t)i+ddt(t2−5)j+ddt(3t−1)k=121+ti+2tj+3k

Then, we evaluate r′(t) at t=3:

r′(3)=121+(3)i+2(3)j+3k=124i+2⋅3j+3k=14i+6j+3k

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point P(2,4,8) is
R(u)=2i+4j+8k+u(14i+6j+3k),u∈(−∞,∞).

q-33491.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)={e}^{t}\,i+3t\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,k$ at the point corresponding to $t=\pi ,$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
q-33491.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=\pi $,  the vector ${r}^{′}(\pi )$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

$$
R(u)=r(\pi )+u{r}^{′}(\pi ),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\pi ) & ={e}^{\pi }\,i+3(\pi )\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡2(\pi )\,k \\  & ={e}^{\pi }\,i+3\pi \,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)\,k \\  & ={e}^{t}\,i+3\,j-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\pi ) & ={e}^{(\pi )}\,i+3\,j+\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡2(\pi )k \\  & ={e}^{\pi }\,i+3\,j\end{aligned}
$$

  

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point 
 where $t=\pi $ is 

$$
R(u)={e}^{\pi }\,i+3\pi \,j+\,k+u({e}^{\pi }\,i+3\,j),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

q-75202.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=⟨\frac{1}{t}-t\,,\frac{1}{t}+t\,⟩$ at the point $P(0,2),$ valid for all real values of $u?$
q-75202.worked_solution:
The point $P(0,2)$  is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point,  the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

$$
R(u)=r({t}_{0})+u\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨0,\,2⟩ \\ ⟨\frac{1}{t}-t\,,\frac{1}{t}+t⟩ & =⟨0,\,2⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the components yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{t}-t=0 \\ \frac{1}{t}+t=2\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Subtracting the first equation from the second, we get $2t=2,$ hence $t=1.$ This value also satisfies both equations. Therefore,  $P(0,2)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(1).$

We calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t}-t)\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t}+t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}-1,\,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}+1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(1) & =⟨-\frac{1}{{1}^{2}}-1,\,-\frac{1}{{1}^{2}}+1⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point  $P(0,2)$ is

$$
R(u)=⟨0\,,\,2⟩+u⟨-2\,,\,0⟩,\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

r(t)=⟨0,2⟩⟨1t−t,1t+t⟩=⟨0,2⟩,

and equating the components yields the following system:

{1t−t=01t+t=2

Subtracting the first equation from the second, we get 2t=2, hence t=1. This value also satisfies both equations. Therefore, P(0,2) is at the tip of the vector r(1).

We calculate r′(t): r′(t)=⟨ddt(1t−t),ddt(1t+t)⟩=⟨−1t2−1,−1t2+1⟩

q-164840.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=({t}^{2}-2)\,i+{t}^{2}\,j,$ $t\in (0,\infty )$, find all of the points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are perpendicular.
q-164840.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j \\  & =2t\,i+2t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ [({t}^{2}-2)\,i+{t}^{2}\,j]\cdot (2t\,i+2t\,j) & =0 \\ ({t}^{2}-2)\cdot 2t+{t}^{2}\cdot 2t & =0 \\ 2t(2{t}^{2}-2) & =0 \\ 4t({t}^{2}-1) & =0 \\ 4t(t-1)(t+1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t\in (0,\infty )$, the only solution is $t=1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =((1)^{2}-2)\,i+(1)^{2}\,j=-\,i+j,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(-1,1).$

Question 11
?

Given the curve r(t)=(t2−2)i+t2j, t∈(0,∞), find all of the points at which r′(t) and r(t) are perpendicular.

a
(−1,1)
b
 (14,16)
c
 (7,9) and (14,16)
d
 (2,4)
e
 (2,4) and (−1,1)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we calculate the derivative of r(t): r′(t)=ddt(t2−2)i+ddt(t2)j=2ti+2tj

The vectors r(t) and r′(t) are perpendicular for some value of the parameter t if and only if r(t)⋅r′(t)=0. So, we have

r(t)⋅r′(t)=0[(t2−2)i+t2j]⋅(2ti+2tj)=0(t2−2)⋅2t+t2⋅2t=02t(2t2−2)=04t(t2−1)=04t(t−1)(t+1)=0.

Since t∈(0,∞), the only solution is t=1.

Finally, since

r(1)=((1)2−2)i+(1)2j=−i+j,

we conclude that r(t) and r′(t) are perpendicular at the point (−1,1).

q-75524.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩,t\in [0,\pi )$ find all of the points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are perpendicular.
q-75524.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,,\,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors  $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\cdot ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,,\,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t) & =0 \\ -8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡2t & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t\in [0,\pi )$, the only solutions are $t=0$ and $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡0\,,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡0⟩=⟨0\,,\,3⟩, \\ r(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}\,,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}⟩=⟨1\,,\,0⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the points $(0,3)$ and $(1,0).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1)\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t\,,\,3{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors  $⟨2\,,\,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨2\,,\,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨2\,,\,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨2\,,\,1⟩\cdot ⟨2t\,,\,3{t}^{2}⟩ & =0 \\ 2\cdot 2t+1\cdot 3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ 4t+3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ t(4+3t) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t\in (-\infty ,0)$, the only solution is $t=-\frac{4}{3}$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-\frac{4}{3}) & =⟨{(-\frac{4}{3})}^{2}-1\,,\,{(-\frac{4}{3})}^{3}+1⟩=⟨\frac{7}{9}\,,\,-\frac{37}{27}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $⟨2\,,\,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(\frac{7}{9}\,,\,-\frac{37}{27}).$

q-164833.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨2{t}^{5}\,,\,{t}^{2}-2⟩,$ $t\in (0,\infty ),$ find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $⟨1\,,\,-5⟩.$

First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{5})\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-2)⟩ \\  & =⟨10{t}^{4}\,,\,2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors  $⟨1\,,\,-5⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨1\,,\,-5⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨1\,,\,-5⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨1\,,\,-5⟩\cdot ⟨10{t}^{4}\,,\,2t⟩ & =0 \\ 1\cdot 10{t}^{4}+(-5)\cdot 2t & =0 \\ 10{t}^{4}-10t & =0 \\ 10t({t}^{3}-1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t\in (0,\infty )$, the only solution is $t=1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨2(1)^{5}\,,\,(1)^{2}-2⟩=⟨2\,,\,-1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $⟨1\,,\,-5⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(2\,,\,-1).$

q-164832.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{4}\,,\,\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}⟩,t\in (-\infty ,0)$ find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $⟨1\,,\,4⟩.$
q-164832.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{4})\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨4{t}^{3}\,,\,{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors  $⟨1\,,\,4⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨1\,,\,4⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨1\,,\,4⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨1\,,\,4⟩\cdot ⟨4{t}^{3}\,,\,{t}^{2}⟩ & =0 \\ 1\cdot 4{t}^{3}+4\cdot {t}^{2} & =0 \\ 4{t}^{3}+4{t}^{2} & =0 \\ 4{t}^{2}(t+1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t\in (-\infty ,0)$, the only solution is $t=-1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨{(-1)}^{4}\,,\,\frac{1}{3}(-1)^{3}⟩=⟨1\,,\,-\frac{1}{3}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $⟨1\,,\,4⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(1\,,\,-\frac{1}{3}).$

q-165039.name: Question 16
q-165039.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}+4t,3{t}^{2}+9t⟩,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨1,3⟩.$
q-165039.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}+4t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}+9t)⟩ \\  & =⟨3t+4,6t+9⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c⟨1,3⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c⟨1,3⟩ \\ ⟨3t+4,6t+9⟩ & =c⟨1,3⟩ \\ ⟨3t+4,6t+9⟩ & =⟨c,3c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3t+4=c \\ 6t+9=3c\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $c=3t+4.$ Substituting $c=3t+4$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6t+9 & =3(3t+4) \\ 6t+9 & =9t+12 \\ 3t & =-3 \\ t & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $⟨1,3⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=-1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨\frac{3}{2}(-1)^{2}+4(-1),3(-1)^{2}+9(-1)⟩=⟨-\frac{5}{2},-6⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨1,3⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(-\frac{5}{2},-6).$

q-165044.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=\frac{1}{t}\,i+({t}^{2}-3)\,j,$ $t\in (0,\infty ),$ find all points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel.
q-165044.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-3)\,j \\  & =-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ \frac{1}{t}\,i+({t}^{2}-3)\,j & =c(-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}i+2t\,j) \\ \frac{1}{t}\,i+({t}^{2}-3)\,j & =-\frac{c}{{t}^{2}}i+2ct\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j$ gives:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{t}=-\frac{c}{{t}^{2}} \\ {t}^{2}-3=2ct\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation we obtain $-t=c.$ Substituting $c=-t$ into the second equality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-3 & =-2{t}^{2} \\ 3{t}^{2}-3 & =0 \\ 3(t+1)(t-1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t\in (0,\infty )$, the only solution is $t=1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =\frac{1}{1}\,i+({1}^{2}-3)\,j \\  & =\,i-2\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(1,-2).$

q-165040.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}-2t\,,\,{t}^{2}\,,\,8t-2{t}^{2}⟩,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨1\,,\,2\,,\,0⟩.$
q-165040.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8t-2{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2t-2,\,2t,\,8-4t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c\,⟨1\,,\,2\,,\,0⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c\,⟨1\,,\,2\,,\,0⟩ \\ ⟨2t-2,\,2t,\,8-4t⟩ & =c\,⟨1\,,\,2\,,\,0⟩ \\ ⟨2t-2,\,2t,\,8-4t⟩ & =⟨c\,,\,2c\,,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2t-2=c \\ 2t=2c \\ 8-4t=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we obtain that $t=2.$ Substituting to the second equation, we get $c=2.$
These values also satisfy the first equation. 

Therefore, $⟨1\,,\,2\,,\,0⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=2.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2) & =⟨{2}^{2}-2(2)\,,\,{2}^{2}\,,\,8(2)-2(2)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,4,\,8⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨1\,,\,2\,,\,0⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(0,4,8).$

q-165038.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{5}-8,2{t}^{4}-6⟩,$ $t\in (0,\infty )$, find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨1,\frac{4}{5}⟩.$
q-165038.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{5}-8),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{4}-6)⟩ \\  & =⟨5{t}^{4},8{t}^{3}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨1,\frac{4}{5}⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c⟨1,\frac{4}{5}⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c⟨1,\frac{4}{5}⟩ \\ ⟨5{t}^{4},8{t}^{3}⟩ & =c⟨1,\frac{4}{5}⟩ \\ ⟨5{t}^{4},8{t}^{3}⟩ & =⟨c,\frac{4c}{5}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}5{t}^{4}=c \\ 8{t}^{3}=\frac{4c}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $c=5{t}^{4}.$ Substituting $c=5{t}^{4}$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}8{t}^{3} & =\frac{4(5{t}^{4})}{5} \\ 8{t}^{3}-4{t}^{4} & =0 \\ 4{t}^{3}(2-t) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t\in (0,\infty )$, the only solution is $t=2.$ 

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2) & =⟨(2)^{5}-8,2(2)^{4}-6⟩=⟨24,26⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨1,\frac{4}{5}⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(24,26).$
